content:
Hi, everyone!

My name is Álvaro Begué. I used to know a bit of math but that was a long time ago. I am primarily a programmer now.

With heavy LLM help, I've managed to formalize the Jordan Curve Theorem and the much harder Jordan-Schönflies theorem.

theorem jordan_schoenflies_of_homeomorph_unconditional
    (hC : IsJordanCurve C) (hC' : IsJordanCurve C') (e : ↥C ≃ₜ ↥C') :
    ∃ F : Plane ≃ₜ Plane, ∀ z : ↥C, F z = e z

I think someone might find this interesting.

https://github.com/alonamaloh/schoenflies-lean

Not to rain on your parade (this is cool! it's lovely to see theorems being formalized, and people discovering they can use AI to do so), but what do we do with this next?

If you give it a #formalization.yaml and setup it up with #comparator, there is the possibility that a human will look at it. (WIthout these, probably no one will, to be realistic.)

But even better, can we turn this in reusable mathematics? Would you be interested in writing, helping write, or reviewing a roadmap for the Tau Ceti project, so we can then start migrating it in?

Thanks for the feedback. I'm not familiar with the conventions that would make this work most useful. But I am happy to learn.

I'll work on following your advice and report back.
I, for one, can reuse this in another AI-assisted formalization project. Thank you!

Coincidentally @Ryan McCorvie formalized the LeanEval version a few days ago at https://github.com/mccorvie/classification-of-surfaces/pull/85 and it passed LeanEval. It's in the classification of surfaces repo but I don't know the level of code reuse.

That's really neat!

My aim was to formalize classification of surfaces. But in Edwin Moise "Geometric Topology in Dimensions 2 and 3", the chapter after triangulation of surfaces is the Schoenflies theorem, and since it was a lean-eval I proved this one too. Since my agent did a lot of pre-reqs in early chapters (~90k loc to prove triangulation), I thought it would be short work. But it took an additional 60k lines to prove Schoenflies. I see your proof is ~70k. I think there is a reason this is one of the later lean-eval problems to fall.

It's interesting you chose to follow Thomassen. For triangulation, I asked LLM's to evaluate that text and Moise for amenability to formalization, and it strongly recommended Moise as being more combinatorial.

Level 11 of the Tau Ceti roadmap for GeometricTopology includes a lot of the topics from Moise including triangulation, but I don't think Schoenflies is directly mentioned. I suspect this roadmap is the right place for Schoenflies, or maybe there should be a separate roadmap for planar topology.
